correctness.rationale: Direct decomposition into iid triangle excursions proves the per-leaf 3/(4n) and per-pair 1/n selection hazards. Exact inclusion-exclusion and an independent finite-state Markov recurrence match in 96 cases. Poisson splitting yields the exact product CDF; Taylor expansion yields a nonzero n^(-1/3) term. De-Poissonization and geometric-excursion maximal concentration have o(n^(-1/3)) distributional errors. Uniform tail domination justifies expectation integration and the n^(2/3) coefficient. The stopped-excursion identity is checked against full random-walk Markov linear systems at n=1,2,3. The packaged checker passed 137 comparisons. Finite experiments are not claimed as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The sharp pointwise positive n^(-1/3) CDF correction and negative explicit n^(2/3) mean term for backtracking cover times on friendship graphs were not found in relevant primary literature, public research indexing or compared mathematical statements. Exact finite-graph inclusion-exclusion, generalized batch coupon expectation, generic Gumbel limits, and first-order n log n network cover times are earlier and are expressly not asserted as novel. Non-backtracking motion on petal cycles concerns a different transition law. Historical priority is best-knowledge, not independently certified.
residual_risks: The broad historical literature on random walks on joined cliques and nonuniform group coupon-collector asymptotics cannot be exhaustively ruled out.
Negative semantic search results are not proof of priority.

value.rationale: The graph is a canonical sparse triangle windmill, and the first-order n log n cover scale hides distinct rare modes of unfinished exploration. The second-order law quantifies the unentered-triangle obstruction, yields an explicit order n^(2/3) expected-cover-time correction, and provides a mathematically motivated benchmark for excursion-based cover-process asymptotics. The precise coefficient is not a routine fixed-n statistic or a known-table recomputation.
